IRAN 255A.description: Examines the visual and religious history of the region defined as "India" today, but necessarily encompassing modern Bangladesh and Pakistan. Culminates with the supposed Golden Age of the Gupta empire and its far-reaching legacies.

IRAN 255B.title: Medieval India
IRAN 255B.description: Begins with the Gupta period's aesthetic legacies in South Asia's architecture, sculpture, and painting. Explores the dispersal of Islam throughout South Asia, including the Muslim communities of southern India.

IRAN 280.title: Studies in Old Iranian
IRAN 280.description: Studies in grammars and texts of Old Persian and Avestan.

IRAN 281.title: Studies in Middle Iranian
IRAN 281.description: Studies in grammars and texts of Middle Iranian languages (e.g., Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, Bactrian).

IRAN 282.title: Studies in Classical Persian
IRAN 282.description: Studies in the premodern literatures and historical texts of medieval and early modern Persian.

IRAN 290.title: Special Topics in Premodern Iranian Studies
IRAN 290.description: Studies in selected areas of premodern Iranian Studies. Topics addressed vary each quarter

IRAN 292.title: Seminar in Premodern Iranian Studies
IRAN 292.description: Seminar in selected areas of premodern Iranian Studies. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

IRAN 293.title: Directed Readings in Premodern Iranian Studies
IRAN 293.description: Directed reading on a specific topic agreed upon by student and instructor.

IRAN 294.title: Curatorial Methods
IRAN 294.description: Development of curatorial methodologies with an instructor in conjunction with curatorial internship or practicum.

IRAN 295.title: Special Methods
IRAN 295.description: Reading course focused on the development of particular research skills (e.g. archaeological field methods, numismatics, digital humanities) often in conjunction with a practicum.

IRAN 296.title: Ethics, Law, and Art
IRAN 296.description: Addresses a broad range of ethical and legal issues pertaining to art, ownership, looting and theft, museum policies, and cultural heritage.
IRAN 296.prereq_text: Background in art history or legal studies.

IRAN 297.title: Directed Readings in Persian/Iranian Studies
IRAN 297.description: Directed reading on a specific topic agreed upon by student and instructor.

IRAN 298.title: Special Topics in Persian/Iranian Studies
IRAN 298.description: Studies in selected areas of Persian/Iranian Studies. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

ITALIAN 1A.title: Fundamentals of Italian
ITALIAN 1A.description: First quarter of first-year Italian in a hybrid or online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.

ITALIAN 1AB.title: Intensive Fundamentals of Italian
ITALIAN 1AB.description: First half of first-year Italian in a time-intensive form. Development of meaningful communicative skills for the purposes of interaction with Italian speakers and beginning study of Italian. Learner-centered approach develops speaking, listening, reading, writing, and cultural skills and knowledge.

ITALIAN 1ABSP.title: Accelerated Fundamentals of Italian for Spanish Speakers
ITALIAN 1ABSP.description: Accelerated first half of first-year Italian for Hispanophone students. Teaches conceptualizing in Italian while learning to read, write, and speak using knowledge of Spanish. Develops awareness of and sensibility to Italian life and culture through reading, viewing, and discussing.
ITALIAN 1ABSP.prereq_text: Two years of high school Spanish, one semester of college Spanish, or heritage speaker of Spanish.

ITALIAN 1B.title: Fundamentals of Italian
ITALIAN 1B.description: Second quarter of first-year Italian in a hybrid or online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.
ITALIAN 1B.prereq_text: ITALIAN 1A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into ITALIAN 1B is also accepted.

ITALIAN 1BC.title: Intensive Fundamentals of Italian
ITALIAN 1BC.description: Second half of first-year Italian in a time-intensive form. Development of meaningful communicative skills for the purposes of interaction with Italian speakers and beginning study of Italian. Learner-centered approach develops speaking, listening, reading, writing, and cultural skills and knowledge.
ITALIAN 1BC.prereq_text: ITALIAN 1AB with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1ABSP with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into ITALIAN 1BC is also accepted.

ITALIAN 1BCSP.title: Accelerated Fundamentals of Italian for Spanish Speakers
ITALIAN 1BCSP.description: Accelerated second half of first-year Italian for Hispanophone students. Teaches conceptualizing in Italian while learning to read, write, and speak using knowledge of Spanish. Develops awareness of and sensibility to Italian life and culture through reading, viewing, and discussing.
ITALIAN 1BCSP.prereq_text: ITALIAN 1ABSP with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1AB with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN S1AB with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1B with a minimum grade of C. Two years of high school Spanish, one semester of college Spanish, or heritage speaker of Spanish.

ITALIAN 1C.title: Fundamentals of Italian
ITALIAN 1C.description: Third quarter of first-year Italian in a hybrid or online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.
ITALIAN 1C.prereq_text: ITALIAN 1B with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1AB with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN S1AB with a minimum grade of C. Placement into ITALIAN 1C is also accepted.

ITALIAN 2A.title: Intermediate Italian
ITALIAN 2A.description: First quarter of second-year Italian in a hybrid or fully online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.
ITALIAN 2A.prereq_text: ITALIAN 1C with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1BC with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN S1BC with a minimum grade of C or ITALIAN 1BCSP with a minimum grade of C. Placement into ITALIAN 2A is also accepted.
ITALIAN 2A.restriction: International Studies majors and School of Humanities students have the first consideration for enrollment.

ITALIAN 2B.title: Intermediate Italian
ITALIAN 2B.description: Second quarter of second-year Italian in a hybrid or fully online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.
ITALIAN 2B.prereq_text: ITALIAN 2A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into ITALIAN 2B is also accepted.
ITALIAN 2B.restriction: International Studies majors and School of Humanities students have the first consideration for enrollment.

ITALIAN 2C.title: Intermediate Italian
ITALIAN 2C.description: Third quarter of second-year Italian in a hybrid and fully online format. Students are taught to conceptualize in Italian as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Classes are conducted entirely in Italian.
ITALIAN 2C.prereq_text: ITALIAN 2B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into 2C is also accepted.
ITALIAN 2C.restriction: School of Humanities students have the first consideration for enrollment.

ITALIAN 50.title: Topics in Italian Culture
ITALIAN 50.description: Examines Italian culture at home and from abroad, in cinema, literature, and popular culture.

ITALIAN 99.title: Special Studies in Italian
ITALIAN 99.description: Both student and instructor arrive at the theme of the course and the critical approach to be followed in consultation. Intended to offer courses in Italian otherwise unavailable.

ITALIAN 150.title: Topics in Italian Literature and Culture
ITALIAN 150.description: Major themes, periods, and/or movements in Italian literature and culture. Taught in English.

ITALIAN 199.title: Independent Study
ITALIAN 199.description: Faculty-guided study of an Italian topic.

JAPANSE 1A.title: Fundamental Japanese
JAPANSE 1A.description: Students develop listening, speaking, reading, and writing abilities in Japanese for meaningful communication. Content deals with daily life, society, and culture in Japan. Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the hiragana and katakana orthography.
JAPANSE 1A.restriction: JAPANSE 1A and JAPANSE S1AB may not be taken for full credit.

JAPANSE 1B.title: Fundamental Japanese
JAPANSE 1B.description: Students develop listening, speaking, reading, and writing abilities in Japanese for meaningful communication. Content deals with daily life, society, and culture in Japan. Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the hiragana and katakana orthography.
JAPANSE 1B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 1A with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE S1AB with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 1B is also accepted.
JAPANSE 1B.restriction: JAPANSE 1B and JAPANSE S1AB and JAPANSE S1BC may not be taken for full credit.

JAPANSE 1C.title: Fundamental Japanese

Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the hiragana and katakana orthography.

JAPANSE S1AB.title: Fundamentals of Japanese
JAPANSE S1AB.description: First half of first-year Japanese in an intensified form.
JAPANSE S1AB.restriction: Students with credit for JAPANSE 1B may not receive full credit for JAPANSE S1AB.

JAPANSE S1BC.title: Fundamentals of Japanese
JAPANSE S1BC.description: Second half of first-year Japanese in an intensified form.
JAPANSE S1BC.prereq_text: JAPANSE S1AB with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE 1B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 1C is also accepted.
JAPANSE S1BC.restriction: Students with credit for JAPANSE 1B may not receive full credit for JAPANSE S1BC.

JAPANSE 2A.title: Intermediate Japanese
JAPANSE 2A.description: Japanese listening, speaking, reading, and writing abilities developed for meaningful communication. Content deals with daily life, society, and culture, including social issues in Japan. Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the 180 characters learned in 1A-B-C.
JAPANSE 2A.prereq_text: JAPANSE 1C with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE S1BC with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 2A is also accepted.
JAPANSE 2A.restriction: JAPANSE 2A and JAPANSE S2AB may not be taken for full credit.

JAPANSE 2B.title: Intermediate Japanese
JAPANSE 2B.description: Japanese listening, speaking, reading, and writing abilities developed for meaningful communication. Content deals with daily life, society, and culture, including social issues in Japan. Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the 180 characters learned in 1A-B-C.
JAPANSE 2B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 2A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 2B is also accepted.
JAPANSE 2B.restriction: JAPANSE 2B and JAPANSE S2AB and JAPANSE S2BC may not be taken for full credit.

JAPANSE 2C.title: Intermediate Japanese
JAPANSE 2C.description: Japanese listening, speaking, reading, and writing abilities developed for meaningful communication. Content deals with daily life, society, and culture, including social issues in Japan. Approximately 180 kanji (Chinese characters) are introduced in addition to the 180 characters learned in 1A-B-C.
JAPANSE 2C.prereq_text: JAPANSE 2B with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE S2AB with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 2C is also accepted.
JAPANSE 2C.restriction: JAPANSE 2C and JAPANSE S2BC may not be taken for full credit.

JAPANSE S2AB.title: Intermediate Japanese
JAPANSE S2AB.description: First half of second-year Japanese in an intensified form.
JAPANSE S2AB.prereq_text: JAPANSE 1C with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE S1BC with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 2A is also accepted.

JAPANSE S2BC.title: Intermediate Japanese
JAPANSE S2BC.description: Second half of second-year Japanese in an intensified form.
JAPANSE S2BC.prereq_text: JAPANSE S2AB with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE 2B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 2C is also accepted.
JAPANSE S2BC.restriction: Students with credit for JAPANSE 2B may not receive full credit for JAPANSE S2BC.

JAPANSE 10.title: Learning Assistant Program
JAPANSE 10.description: Learning Assistant Program in which students at an advanced level of Japanese (JAPANSE 103A or above) provide assistance to students at fundamentals (JAPANSE 1A-B-C).

JAPANSE 100A.title: Classical Japanese
JAPANSE 100A.description: Introduction to classical Japanese grammar and vocabulary with emphasis on reading and analysis of basic texts.
JAPANSE 100A.prereq_text: JAPANSE 103C with a minimum grade of C.

JAPANSE 100B.title: Classical Japanese
JAPANSE 100B.description: Introduction to classical Japanese grammar and vocabulary with emphasis on reading and analysis of basic texts.
JAPANSE 100B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 100A with a minimum grade of C.

JAPANSE 103A.title: Advanced Japanese
JAPANSE 103A.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Japanese as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Authentic Japanese texts are used. Approximately 360 kanji (Chinese characters) and the 270 characters learned in the first and second years are introduced.
JAPANSE 103A.prereq_text: JAPANSE 2C with a minimum grade of C or JAPANSE S2BC with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 103A is also accepted.

JAPANSE 103B.title: Advanced Japanese
JAPANSE 103B.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Japanese as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Authentic Japanese texts are used. Approximately 360 kanji (Chinese characters) and the 270 characters learned in the first and second years are introduced.
JAPANSE 103B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 103A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 103B is also accepted.

JAPANSE 103C.title: Advanced Japanese
JAPANSE 103C.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Japanese as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Authentic Japanese texts are used. Approximately 360 kanji (Chinese characters) and the 270 characters learned in the first and second years are introduced.
JAPANSE 103C.prereq_text: JAPANSE 103B (may be taken concurrently) with a minimum grade of C. Placement into JAPANSE 103C is also accepted.
JAPANSE 103C.restriction: Japanese Language and Literature majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

JAPANSE 104A.title: Fourth Year Japanese
JAPANSE 104A.description: Continued emphasis on comprehension, grammar, and proficiency in reading, composition, and conversation through intensive study and analysis of a variety of texts.

JAPANSE 104B.title: Fourth Year Japanese
JAPANSE 104B.description: Continued emphasis on comprehension, grammar, and proficiency in reading, composition, and conversation through intensive study and analysis of a variety of texts.

JAPANSE 199.title: Independent Study
JAPANSE 199.description: Investigation of special topics through directed reading in Japanese. Paper required.

JAPANSE 203.title: Readings in Modern Japanese Literature
JAPANSE 203.description: Texts include both fiction and nonfiction by important writers, and may be supplemented where needed by literary criticism and cultural-studies texts in English.

JAPANSE 211B.title: Studies in Traditional Japanese Prose
JAPANSE 211B.description: Studies in selected areas of traditional Japanese prose. Topics addressed vary each quarter. Research paper required.
JAPANSE 211B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 100B and JAPANSE 211A with a minimum grade of B-.

JAPANSE 212A.title: Studies in Traditional Japanese Poetry or Drama
JAPANSE 212A.description: Studies in selected areas of traditional Japanese poetry or drama. Topics addressed vary each quarter. Research paper required.

JAPANSE 213B.title: Studies in Modern Japanese Literature
JAPANSE 213B.description: A two-quarter, in-depth look at a major author and/or issue in modern Japanese literature. Seminar format. The first quarter is devoted to reading of the requisite texts; the second quarter, to the writing of a research paper.
JAPANSE 213B.prereq_text: JAPANSE 203 with a minimum grade of B- and JAPANSE 213A with a minimum grade of B-.

JAPANSE 215.title: Studies in Japanese Religion
JAPANSE 215.description: Studies in selected areas of Japanese religion. Topics addressed vary each quarter. Research paper required.

JAPANSE 290.title: Independent Study
JAPANSE 290.description: Directed research on topic determined in consultation with faculty member. A term paper or project is required.

JAPANSE 299.title: Dissertation Research
JAPANSE 299.description: For Students who have been admitted to doctoral candidacy.

KOREAN 1B.title: Fundamental Korean
KOREAN 1B.description: Natural approach with emphasis on the four fundamental skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing for students with no previous background in Korean. Conducted in both English and Korean.
KOREAN 1B.prereq_text: KOREAN 1A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 1B is also accepted.

KOREAN 1C.title: Fundamental Korean

KOREAN 1C.prereq_text: KOREAN 1B with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN S1AB with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 1C is also accepted.

KOREAN S1AB.title: Fundamentals of Korean
KOREAN S1AB.description: First half of first-year Korean in an intensified form.
KOREAN S1AB.restriction: Students with credit for KOREAN 1B may not receive full credit for KOREAN S1AB.

KOREAN S1BC.title: Fundamentals of Korean
KOREAN S1BC.description: Second half of first-year Korean in an intensified form.
KOREAN S1BC.prereq_text: KOREAN S1AB with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 1B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 1C is also accepted.
KOREAN S1BC.restriction: Students with credit for KOREAN 1B may not receive full credit for KOREAN S1BC.

KOREAN 2A.title: Intermediate Korean
KOREAN 2A.description: Designed to develop writing and reading skills as well as communicative skills in authentic situations for students without previous initial background in Korean. Students also introduced to aspects of Korean culture as related to lesson topics and basic Chinese characters.

KOREAN 2B.description: Designed to develop writing and reading skills as well as communicative skills in authentic situations for students without previous initial background in Korean. Students also introduced to aspects of Korean culture as related to lesson topics and basic Chinese characters.
KOREAN 2B.prereq_text: KOREAN 2A with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 2B is also accepted.

KOREAN 2C.title: Intermediate Korean
KOREAN 2C.description: Designed to develop writing and reading skills as well as communicative skills in authentic situations for students without previous initial background in Korean. Students also introduced to aspects of Korean culture as related to lesson topics and basic Chinese characters.
KOREAN 2C.prereq_text: KOREAN 2B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 2C is also accepted.

KOREAN 10.title: Learning Assistant Program
KOREAN 10.description: Learning Assistant Program in which students at an advanced level of Korean (KOREAN 103A or above) provide assistance to students at fundamentals (KOREAN 1A-B-C).

KOREAN 103A.title: Advanced Korean
KOREAN 103A.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Korean as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Focuses on developing advanced reading, writing, and translating skills.
KOREAN 103A.prereq_text: KOREAN 2C with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 2KC with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN S2BC with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 103A is also accepted.

KOREAN 103B.title: Advanced Korean
KOREAN 103B.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Korean as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Focuses on developing advanced reading, writing, and translating skills.
KOREAN 103B.prereq_text: KOREAN 103A with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 2C with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 2KC with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN S2BC with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 103B is also accepted.

KOREAN 103C.title: Advanced Korean
KOREAN 103C.description: Students are taught to conceptualize in Korean as they learn to understand, read, write, and speak. Focuses on developing advanced reading, writing, and translating skills.
KOREAN 103C.prereq_text: KOREAN 2C with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 2KC with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN S2BC with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 103A with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 103B with a minimum grade of C. Placement into KOREAN 103C is also accepted.

KOREAN 104A.title: Fourth-Year Korean
KOREAN 104A.description: Continued emphasis on comprehension, grammar, and proficiency in reading, composition, and conversation through intensive study and analysis of a variety of modern texts.
KOREAN 104A.prereq_text: KOREAN 103A with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 103B with a minimum grade of C or KOREAN 103C with a minimum grade of C.

KOREAN 199.title: Independent Study
KOREAN 199.description: Investigation of special topics through directed reading in Korean. Paper required.

LATIN 1A.title: Fundamentals of Latin
LATIN 1A.description: Elements of Latin grammar, syntax, and vocabulary.
LATIN 1A.restriction: LATIN 1A and LATIN S1AB may not be taken for full credit.

LATIN 1B.title: Fundamentals of Latin
LATIN 1B.description: Elements of Latin grammar, syntax, and vocabulary.
LATIN 1B.prereq_text: LATIN 1A with a minimum grade of C.
LATIN 1B.restriction: LATIN 1B and LATIN S1AB and LATIN S1BC may not be taken for full credit.

LATIN 1C.title: Fundamentals of Latin
LATIN 1C.description: Introduction to reading texts, including study of the poetry of Catullus and selected readings.
LATIN 1C.prereq_text: LATIN 1B with a minimum grade of C.
LATIN 1C.restriction: LATIN 1C and LATIN S1BC may not be taken for full credit.

LATIN 99.title: Special Studies in Latin
LATIN 99.description: Lower-division level independent research with Latin faculty.

LATIN 100.title: Topics in Classical Latin
LATIN 100.description: Selected readings in Classical Latin prose and poetry. Authors may include Cicero, Caesar, Ovid, Catullus, and others. Selections from prose and poetry will be read each quarter. Grammar and syntax review included.
LATIN 100.prereq_text: LATIN 1C with a minimum grade of C. Placement into Latin 100 is also accepted.

LATIN 103.title: Seminar in Latin Prose
LATIN 103.description: Specialized and focused study of a particular Latin prose author or topic.

LATIN 104.title: Seminar in Latin Poetry
LATIN 104.description: Specialized and focused study of a particular topic or author in Latin poetry.

LATIN 198.title: Directed Group Study
LATIN 198.description: Special topics in Roman culture and civilization through directed reading and research.

LIT JRN 20.title: Introduction to Literary Journalism
LIT JRN 20.description: Reading of selected texts to explore the ways in which literary journalism and related nonfiction modes formulate experience. Students complete a range of writing projects.
LIT JRN 20.prereq_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.
LIT JRN 20.restriction: Literary Journalism majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LIT JRN 21.title: Reporting for Literary Journalism
LIT JRN 21.description: Instruction and hands-on training in how to interview, report, research, and collect the types of information needed to write literary journalism.
LIT JRN 21.prereq_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.
LIT JRN 21.restriction: Literary Journalism majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LIT JRN 100.title: Advanced Reporting
LIT JRN 100.description: Practical engagement with advanced reporting techniques of Literary Journalism, emphasizing the importance of thorough and effective research in the production of high-quality journalistic writing. Prepares students to make good decisions about where and how to publish their writing.

LIT JRN 101A.title: Studies in the History, Theory, and Ethics of Literary Journalism
LIT JRN 101A.description: Lectures and discussion on topics that explore the historical and theoretical dimensions of literary journalism, with particular emphasis on the evolution of ethics in the field.
LIT JRN 101A.prereq_text: LIT JRN 21 and LIT JRN 20 and (COM LIT 60A or COM LIT 60C or ENGLISH 8 or ENGLISH 9 or ENGLISH 10 or ENGLISH 11 or ENGLISH 12 or ENGLISH 15 or ENGLISH 16 or ENGLISH 17).

LIT JRN 101BW.title: Literary Journalism Core Writing Workshop
LIT JRN 101BW.description: Writing workshops in announced specialized genres that students will both study and practice. Examples include "The Memoir," "Review Writing," "The Editorial," "Writing Biography," "The Profile," and "Political Writing."
LIT JRN 101BW.prereq_text: LIT JRN 101A. Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.
LIT JRN 101BW.restriction: Students may enroll in one LITJ 101BW course per quarter.

LIT JRN 103.title: Lectures on Topics in Literary Journalism
LIT JRN 103.description: A series of lectures on, and discussions of, announced topics in literary journalism and the literature of fact. Examples include "Travel Literary Journalism"; "Literature of True Crime"; "Narratives in the Digital Age"; "Journalism on the Edge".
LIT JRN 103.prereq_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

LIT JRN 198.title: Special Topics
LIT JRN 198.description: Directed group study of selected topics.

LIT JRN 199.title: Reading and Conference
LIT JRN 199.description: To be taken only when the materials to be studied lie outside the normal run of departmental offerings.

LPS 19.title: AI Literacy
LPS 19.description: Introduction to the basics of contemporary artificial intelligence. Distinction between symbolic and neural AIs. Generative AI, prediction engines, recommendation systems, machine perception. Near-term ethical issues, medium-term economic implications, long-term risk, and safety.

LPS 29.title: Critical Reasoning
LPS 29.description: Introduction to analysis and reasoning. The concepts of argument, premise, and conclusion, validity and invalidity, consistency and inconsistency. Identifying and assessing premises and inferences. Deductive versus inductive reasoning, and introduction to the probability calculus. Evaluating definitions. Informal fallacies.

LPS 30.title: Introduction to Symbolic Logic
LPS 30.description: An introduction to the symbolism and methods of the logic of statements, including evaluation of arguments by truth tables, the techniques of natural deduction, and semantic tableaux.

LPS 31.title: Introduction to Inductive Logic
LPS 31.description: Philosophical questions concerning the foundations of scientific inference, e.g., the traditional problem of induction, the Goodman paradox, the concept of cause, Mill's method of inductive reasoning, probability calculus, different interpretations of probability, and their interaction in inductive reasoning.

LPS 40.title: The Nature of Scientific Inquiry
LPS 40.description: Investigates the nature, scope, and status of scientific knowledge and the methods used to acquire it. Uses concrete historical examples from a variety of scientific fields to identify distinctive features of the scientific enterprise and explore their significance.

LPS 50.title: Science in the Public Sphere
LPS 50.description: Investigates the role of science in a democratic society. Discusses the scope and limits of scientific knowledge in the context of arguments for the special status of science in political decision-making. Uses concrete historical examples from a variety of fields.

LPS 60.title: The Making of Modern Science
LPS 60.description: Surveys the history of science and mathematics since the Scientific Revolution, examining central developments both chronologically and thematically, as well as investigating their significance for contemporary philosophical debates about the role and status of current scientific theories.

LPS H81.title: What is Space?
LPS H81.description: Historical, philosophical, scientific exploration of the concept of "space." Questions of interest include: What kind of a thing is space? How can we know what space is like? How is space different from time?

LPS H83.title: Evolutionary Foundations of Human Moral Psychology
LPS H83.description: Examines origin and function(s) of human moral psychology from an evolutionary point of view, drawing on theories and experimental findings from evolutionary biology, social psychology, developmental and comparative psychology, primatology, anthropology, and philosophy.

LPS 91.title: Sex, Race, and Science
LPS 91.description: Discusses the origins of biological sex, dynamics of sexual selection, sex differences in humans, and the construction of gender in human societies. Seeks to understand the role social values play in the creation of science.

LPS H91.title: The Philosophy and Biology of Sex
LPS H91.description: Covers the origins of biological sex, dynamics of sexual selection, the evolution and cultural creation of sexual behavior in humans, and the construction of gender in human societies.

LPS H95.title: Jurisprudence and Constitutional Law
LPS H95.description: Applies competing theories of the nature of law and legal reasoning to evaluate decisions of the U.S. Supreme Court in controversial areas of constitutional law such as free speech, privacy, sexual conduct, affirmative action, and political campaign contributions.

LPS 100W.title: Writing Philosophy
LPS 100W.description: Discussion of those aspects of writing of special importance in philosophy, e.g., philosophical terminology, techniques for evaluating arguments, philosophical definitions and theories. At least 4,000 words of assigned composition based on philosophical readings.
LPS 100W.prereq_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

LPS 104.title: Introduction to Logic
LPS 104.description: Introduction to sentence logic, including truth tables and natural deduction; and to predicate logic, including semantics and natural deduction.

LPS 105A.title: Introduction to Set Theory and Mathematical Reasoning
LPS 105A.description: An introduction to the basic working vocabulary of mathematical reasoning and proof. Topics include sets, Boolean operations, ordered n-tuples, relations, functions, induction, and their applications to mathematical philosophy.

LPS 105B.title: Metalogic
LPS 105B.description: Introduction to formal syntax (proof theory) and semantics (model theory) for first-order logic, including the deduction, completeness, compactness, and Löewenheim-Skolem theorems.

LPS 105C.title: Undecidability and Incompleteness
LPS 105C.description: Introduction to the formal theory of effective processes, including recursive functions, Turing machines, Church's thesis, and proofs of Göedel's incompleteness theorem for arithmetic, and Church's undecidability theorem for first-order logic.

LPS 106.title: Topics in Logic
LPS 106.description: Selected topics in mathematical or philosophical logic.
LPS 106.prereq_text: (LPS 105A or PHILOS 105A or LSCI 145A) and (LPS 105B or PHILOS 105B or LSCI 145B) and (LPS 105C or PHILOS 105C or LSCI 145C).

LPS 108.title: Topics in Induction, Probability, and Decision Theory
LPS 108.description: Selected topics in induction, probability, and decision theory.

LPS 113.title: Topics in Modern Philosophy
LPS 113.description: Focuses on the works of central philosophical figures of modern Philosophy (e.g., Descartes, Leibniz, Hobbes, Locke, Hume, Kant) or on the treatment of one or more central philosophical problems by a number of these figures.

LPS 115.title: Topics in History of Analytic Philosophy
LPS 115.description: Review of central theories or figures in the history of analytic philosophy. Emphasis on writings of Frege, Russell, Schlick, Carnap, and Quine. Topics include the nature of meaning and truth, the synthetic/analytic distinction, and scientific knowledge.

LPS 120.title: Topics in Metaphysics
LPS 120.description: Examines central philosophical questions concerning our own fundamental nature and that of the world around us (e.g., causation and necessity, determination, free will, personal identity, the mind-body problem).

LPS 121.title: Topics in the Theory of Knowledge
LPS 121.description: One or more topics in the theory of knowledge, e.g., the nature of rational justification, of perceptual knowledge, of a priori knowledge.

LPS H123.title: What is Disease?
LPS H123.description: Explores philosophical issues associated with scientific efforts to understand and explain disease.

LPS H125.title: What Is Time?
LPS H125.description: Engages the question "what is time?" by drawing on physics, philosophy, fiction, film, and psychology. Organized around understanding and addressing the tension between time as represented in physics and our immediate temporal experience.

LPS 135A.title: The Scientific Revolution
LPS 135A.description: An examination of early modern European science from 1500-1700. Includes primary readings from central figures (Copernicus, Harvey, Bacon, Descartes, et al.); themes include the impact of printing, humanism, patronage, technology, and discussion of the term "revolution" in this context.

LPS 140.title: Topics in Philosophy of Science
LPS 140.description: Selected topics in contemporary philosophy of science, e.g., the status of theoretical entities, the confirmation of theories, the nature of scientific explanation.

LPS 141B.title: Geometry and Spacetime
LPS 141B.description: An examination of the foundations of the special theory of relativity, with emphasis on the geometry of Minkowski spacetime, and its relation to both Euclidean and non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) plane geometries.

LPS 141D.title: Probability and Determinism
LPS 141D.description: An examination of a cluster of interrelated issues concerning probability, determinism, logic, and the foundations of quantum mechanics.

LPS H141.title: Honors Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics
LPS H141.description: An examination of the standard von Neumann-Dirac formulation of quantum mechanics. The quantum measurement problem is discussed along with several proposed solutions, including GRW, many-worlds, man-minds, and Bohm's theory.

LPS 143.title: Topics in Philosophy of Psychology
LPS 143.description: Selected topics in the philosophy of psychology, e.g., the nature of psychological explanation, reductionism, issues in cognitive, behavioral, and neuroscience.
LPS 143.restriction: Philosophy majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LPS 144.title: Topics in Philosophy of Social Science
LPS 144.description: Selected topics in the philosophy of the social sciences, e.g.: Is their goal to understand behavior or to predict and control it? Are they normative and the natural sciences not? Do they incorporate philosophical doctrines about language and mind?

LPS 145.title: Topics in Philosophy of Language
LPS 145.description: Selected topics in the philosophy of language, e.g., the nature of meaning, mechanisms of reference, speech acts.

LPS 147.title: Topics in Philosophy of Mathematics
LPS 147.description: Selected historical and contemporary topics in the philosophy of mathematics, e.g., mathematical truth and ontology, mathematical knowledge, the nature and role of proof, the workings of mathematics in application.

LPS 199.title: Independent Study
LPS 199.description: Independent research with Logic and Philosophy of Science faculty.

LPS 205A.title: Introduction to Set Theory and Mathematical Reasoning
LPS 205A.description: An introduction to the basic working vocabulary of mathematical reasoning and proof. Topics include sets, Boolean operations, ordered n-tuples, relations, functions, induction, and their applications to mathematical philosophy.

LPS 205B.title: Metalogic
LPS 205B.description: Formal syntax (proof theory) and semantics (model theory) for first-order logic, including the deduction, completeness, compactness, and Loewenheim-Skolem theorems.
LPS 205B.prereq_text: PHILOS 205A with a minimum grade of B- or LPS 205A with a minimum grade of B-.

LPS 205C.title: Undecidability and Incompleteness
LPS 205C.description: Formal theory of effective processes, including recursive function, Turing machines, Church's thesis, proofs of Goedel's incompleteness theorem for arithmetics, and Church's undecidability for first-order logic.
LPS 205C.prereq_text: PHILOS 205B with a minimum grade of B- or LPS 205B with a minimum grade of B-.

LPS 206.title: Topics in Logic
LPS 206.description: Studies in selected areas of logic. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 213.title: Topics in Modern Philosophy
LPS 213.description: Studies in selected areas of modern philosophy. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 215.title: Topics in Analytic Philosophy
LPS 215.description: Studies in selected areas of analytic philosophy. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 220.title: Topics in Metaphysics
LPS 220.description: Studies in selected areas of metaphysics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 221.title: Topics in Epistemology
LPS 221.description: Studies in selected areas of epistemology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 221A.title: Medical Epistemology
LPS 221A.description: Analysis of epistemological issues concerning medical research and healthcare. Topics may include medical evidence, transmission of medical knowledge in the doctor-patient interaction, medical expertise, epistemology of medical disagreement, classification of illness, well-being, philosophy of pain, or medical decision making.

LPS 232.title: Topics in Political and Social Philosophy
LPS 232.description: Studies in selected areas of political and social philosophy. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 240.title: Topics in Philosophy of Science
LPS 240.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of science. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 241.title: Topics in Philosophy of Physics
LPS 241.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of physics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 242.title: Topics in Philosophy of Biology
LPS 242.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of biology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 243.title: Topics in Philosophy of Psychology
LPS 243.description: Selected topics in the philosophy of psychology, e.g., the nature of psychological explanation, reductionism, issues in cognitive, behavioral, and neuroscience.

LPS 244.title: Topics in Philosophy of Social Science
LPS 244.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy and social science. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 244A.title: PPE Proseminar I
LPS 244A.description: Introduces tools and concepts useful for working in the intersection of philosophy, political science, and economics. These are drawn from probability theory, decision theory, and the psychology of belief, knowledge, and rational choice.

LPS 244B.title: PPE Proseminar II
LPS 244B.description: Introduces some of the main theoretical topics at the intersection of philosophy, political science, and economics. PPE II covers (1) Rational Choice based game theory, (2) Evolutionary Game Theory, and (3) Voting and Social Choice.

LPS 245.title: Topics in Philosophy of Language
LPS 245.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of language. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 246.title: Topics in Philosophy of Logic
LPS 246.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of logic. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 247.title: Topics in Philosophy of Mathematics
LPS 247.description: Studies in selected areas of philosophy of mathematics. Topics addressed vary each quarter.

LPS 289.title: Logic and Philosophy of Science Workshop
LPS 289.description: A two- or three-quarter-long workshop on selected topics in logic and philosophy of science.

LPS 298.title: Independent Study
LPS 298.description: Independent research with Logic and Philosophy of Science Faculty.

LPS 299.title: Directed Research
LPS 299.description: Directed study with Logic and Philosophy of Science Faculty.

LPS 399.title: University Teaching
LPS 399.description: Required of and limited to Teaching Assistants.

LSCI 1.title: Languages of the World
LSCI 1.description: The world has over 6,000 languages, with an exuberant variety of sounds, words, grammars. Introduction to a representative (about eight), drawn from every continent. Students are not expected to learn languages, but to explore and study their structure and complexity.

LSCI 2.title: Discovering Language
LSCI 2.description: Explores language's pervasiveness and diversity; demonstrates ways linguistics illuminates language's crucial--albeit hidden--societal role. Issues: self-and group-identification, language death, language in legal and educational settings. Illustrations: spoken and signed languages, varieties of English, Native American languages.

LSCI 3.title: Introduction to Linguistics
LSCI 3.description: Emphasis on the notion that language is a remarkable achievement of the human mind. Current insights into the nature of language. Survey of various subfields of linguistics. Introduction to linguistic analysis.

LSCI 10.title: Introduction to Phonology
LSCI 10.description: Basic concepts in phonetic description and phonological analysis.

LSCI 11.title: Introduction to Deaf Culture
LSCI 11.description: Study of varied topics in Deaf culture such as language, identity, traditions, norms, and values. Area studies, and society, both in the present and in historical perspective are also examined. Taught in English.

LSCI 20.title: Introduction to Syntax
LSCI 20.description: Basic concepts in syntactic description and grammatical analysis.

LSCI 43.title: Introduction to Symbolic Logic
LSCI 43.description: An introduction to the symbolism and methods of the logic of statements, including evaluation of arguments by truth tables, the techniques of natural deduction, and semantic tableaux.

LSCI 51.title: Acquisition of Language
LSCI 51.description: What children say, what they mean, and what they understand. Theories about the learning of language by one-, two-, and three-year-olds. Comparison of kinds of data on which these theories are based.

LSCI 51B.title: Foundations of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism
LSCI 51B.description: Provides a comprehensive overview of current issues in bilingual education and bilingualism. Topics include dimensions of bilingualism, the effects of bilingualism on children's linguistic and cognitive development, bilingual education programs, literacy, special needs, and assessment.

LSCI 52.title: Bilingual Minds and Brains
LSCI 52.description: Examines the variation in the languages that are spoken and the social contexts in which they are used may shape the way we communicate. Explore ways emerging science of bilingualism might be better communicated to the public.
LSCI 52.restriction: Education Sciences majors and Language Science majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 68.title: Introduction to Language and Culture
LSCI 68.description: Explores what the study of language can reveal about ourselves as bearers of culture. After introducing some basic concepts, examines how cultural knowledge is linguistically organized and how language might shape our perception of the world.

LSCI 102.title: Formal Languages and Automata
LSCI 102.description: Formal aspects of describing and recognizing languages by grammars and automata. Parsing regular and context-free languages. Ambiguity, nondeterminism. Elements of computability; Turning machines, random access machines, undecidable problems, NP-completeness.
LSCI 102.prereq_text: I&C SCI 46 with a minimum grade of C and (MATH 2B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4) and I&C SCI 6B and I&C SCI 6D.

LSCI 106.title: Topics in Logic
LSCI 106.description: Selected topics in mathematical or philosophical logic.
LSCI 106.prereq_text: (LPS 105A or PHILOS 105A or LSCI 145A) and (LPS 105B or PHILOS 105B or LSCI 145B) and (LPS 105C or PHILOS 105C or LSCI 145C).

LSCI 106M.title: Computational Models of Language Learning
LSCI 106M.description: Focuses on using computational models to investigate questions related to language learning. Topics include computational models of language acquisition, principles underlying models of language learning and language change, computational learning theory, and modeling information extraction from language by humans.
LSCI 106M.prereq_text: LSCI 151 with a minimum grade of A-.

LSCI 107M.title: Computational Methods for Language Research
LSCI 107M.description: Focuses on computational methods useful for language research. Students become familiar with software and programming languages used for extracting information from electronic datasets and for creating basic simulations of linguistic cognition. No prior programming experience assumed.
LSCI 107M.prereq_text: COGS 150 or LSCI 155 or COGS 156A or LSCI 151.
LSCI 107M.restriction: Language Science majors, Cognitive Sciences majors, and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 107P.title: Introduction to Programming for Language Science
LSCI 107P.description: Provides an introduction to the fundamentals of programming in Python, with specific applications for the study of human language. No prior programming knowledge is assumed.
LSCI 107P.prereq_text: LSCI 3 with a minimum grade of C-.
LSCI 107P.restriction: Language Science majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 115.title: Introduction to Phonetics
LSCI 115.description: Introduces students to fundamental concepts of phonetics. The sound systems of selected languages around the world, including that of English, are described in detail. Students are trained to work with speech sound recognition, phonetic transcription, and language sound production.

LSCI 116.title: Introduction to Speech Science
LSCI 116.description: Introduces students to the central topics in speech science and cultivates critical thinking in evaluating scientific literature through lectures, readings, and discussions.

LSCI 117.title: Introduction to Acoustic Phonetics
LSCI 117.description: Introduction to the study of the acoustic properties of speech and their relationship to speech articulation and speech perception. Topics covered include making and interpreting quantitative acoustic measurements of speech, basic experimental design, and basic data visualization and statistical analysis.
LSCI 117.prereq_text: LSCI 3 (may be taken concurrently) and LSCI 10 (may be taken concurrently).

LSCI 124.title: Current Topics in Syntactic Theory
LSCI 124.description: Research seminar in syntax. Intensive study of a small number of well-defined topics which have had significant impact on the development of syntactic theory.

LSCI 141.title: Topics in Philosophy of Language
LSCI 141.description: Selected topics in the philosophy of language, e.g., the nature of meaning, mechanisms of reference, speech acts.

LSCI 142.title: Introduction to Logic
LSCI 142.description: Introduction to sentence logic, including truth tables and natural deduction; and to predicate logic, including semantics and natural deduction.

LSCI 143.title: Introduction to Formal Semantics
LSCI 143.description: Introduces students to the analytical tools used in the investigation of natural language semantics. Topics include the truth-conditional approach to meaning, compositionality, scope and anaphora, generalized quantifier theory, and intensionality.
LSCI 143.prereq_text: LPS 30 with a minimum grade of C- or LSCI 43 with a minimum grade of C- or PHILOS 30 with a minimum grade of C- or LPS 104 with a minimum grade of C- or PHILOS 104 with a minimum grade of C- or LSCI 142 with a minimum grade of C-.

LSCI 145A.title: Elementary Set Theory
LSCI 145A.description: An introduction to the basic working vocabulary of mathematical reasoning. Topics include sets, Boolean operations, ordered n-tuples, relations, functions, ordinal and cardinal numbers.

LSCI 145B.title: Metalogic
LSCI 145B.description: Introduction to formal syntax (proof theory) and semantics (model theory) for first-order logic, including the deduction, completeness, compactness, and Löewenheim-Skolem theorems.
LSCI 145B.prereq_text: PHIL 105A LSCI 145A or LPS 105A or PHILOS 105A.

LSCI 145C.title: Undecidability and Incompleteness
LSCI 145C.description: Introduction to the formal theory of effective processes, including recursive functions, Turing machines, Church's thesis, and proofs of Göedel's incompleteness theorem for arithmetic, and Church's undecidability theorem for first-order logic.
LSCI 145C.prereq_text: PHIL 105B LSCI 145B or LPS 105B or PHILOS 105B.

LSCI 151C.title: Computational Cognitive Models of Language Acquisition
LSCI 151C.description: Focuses on synthesizing research literature related to computational cognitive models of language acquisition. Students develop their abilities to discuss key concepts and background assumptions, clearly present major points and findings, and concisely summarize literature from a particular perspective.

LSCI 151S.title: Second Language Acquisition
LSCI 151S.description: Examines a number of theoretical perspectives that attempt to explain second language learning with a focus on adult learners. How universal constraints, individual differences, and social factors influence the task of learning a second language as an adult.

LSCI 152.title: Acquisition of Language III
LSCI 152.description: Focuses on native language learning, exploring the way in which infants and very young children unconsciously uncover the rich systematic knowledge of their native language. Examines both experimental and computational studies that quantitatively investigate the "how" of language acquisition.

LSCI 153M.title: Experimental Research in Language Science
LSCI 153M.description: Covers foundational topics in behavioral research and experimentation, focusing on examples from language science.
LSCI 153M.restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors and Language Science majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 155.title: Psychology of Language
LSCI 155.description: Examines language using the tools of experimental psychology. From sounds to words to spoken and written sentences, explores how language is used in real time, and how its use reveals how it is represented in the mind.
LSCI 155.restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Language Science majors, and Psychology majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 158.title: Language and the Brain
LSCI 158.description: Research analysis on biological bases of human linguistic capacity. Development, focusing on hemispheric specialization, plasticity; localization of specific linguistic functions in adults, with emphasis on study of aphasias; relation of linguistic capacity to general cognitive capacity, considering research on retardation.
LSCI 158.prereq_text: (PSYC 7A (COGS 7A or PSB 9 or PSCI 9 or PSYC 9A or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4) or PSB 11A) or (COGS 9A and (PSYC 9B or PSCI 11A) or PSB 11B and (COGS 9B or BIOL 35 or PSCI 11B) or BIOL N110) or BIO SCI 35 or BIO SCI N110 or BIO SCI N115A.

LSCI 165B.title: Structure of Japanese
LSCI 165B.description: An overview of the linguistic features of modern Japanese. Provides students with a systematic introduction to the nature and characteristics of the language.

LSCI 165P.title: Prosody of Japanese Poetry and Songs
LSCI 165P.description: Sheds linguistic light on the traditions of Japanese poetry and song that have evolved over more than a thousand years, and demonstrates the central role of phonetic elements in these traditions.
LSCI 165P.restriction: No Language Science majors and No East Asian Cultures majors. No Linguistics minors and No Asian Studies minors.

LSCI 165S.title: Japanese Sociolinguistics
LSCI 165S.description: Introduction to Japanese sociolinguistics, exploring how the variety of language use in modern Japanese is constructed by identity and culture. Topics include language assimilation, dialect use, language formality, codeswitching, backchanneling, politeness, honorifics, and use of gendered language given social norms.
LSCI 165S.restriction: Language Science majors and East Asian Cultures majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 168J.title: Improvisation, Language, and Culture
LSCI 168J.description: Addresses improvisation, both in performance and in everyday life. Examines improvisation as the "flexible regulation" of everyday behavior by exploring different scholarly treatments of language and interaction, and working on developing actual theatrical improvisation skills.

LSCI 168S.title: Language and Social Cognition
LSCI 168S.description: Explores the relationship between language and cognition in social and cultural contexts. The overall goal is to think through how language structure and use impact how individuals perceive, think about, and understand the world around them.

LSCI 171.title: Evolution of Language and Music
LSCI 171.description: Focuses on the biological evolution of two rather unique human traits: language and music. No other species is capable of “doing” language or music with the complexity that humans can.
LSCI 171.prereq_text: COGS 7A or PSY 9 or AP Psychology Exam with a minimum score of 4 or (COGS 9A and COGS 9B) or LSCI 3.
LSCI 171.restriction: Cognitive Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and Language Science majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 172.title: History of English
LSCI 172.description: Traces the history of English from its roots through its earliest written records and into the present, including fundamental changes in morphology, phonology, syntax, semantics, and vocabulary, as well as social, cultural, and historical forces affecting language.

LSCI 175.title: Language Origins: Evolution, Genetics, and the Brain
LSCI 175.description: Examines how human language(s) may have originated. Studies pertinent techniques (reconstruction) and addresses related questions, including is our language faculty inborn (i.e., genetically encoded)? Can brain imaging and population genetics research help to unlock this mystery of human evolution?

LSCI 182V.title: Language and Literacy
LSCI 182V.description: Addresses the linguistic principles and processes that underlie oral and written language proficiency. Emphasis is on how to use phonology, morphology, orthography, semantics, syntax, and pragmatics to support literacy and oral language development for K-12 students.
LSCI 182V.restriction: Language Science majors, Psychological Science majors, Education Sciences majors, Psychology majors, and Social Ecology majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

LSCI 189.title: Special Topics in Applied Language Science: Writing Skills for Language Science

LSCI 195A.title: Language Science Research I
LSCI 195A.description: Provides students with in-depth experience in different facets of research in language science. It includes theoretical, behavioral, computational, and/or applied language science topics and methodologies.
LSCI 195A.prereq_text: Permission of faculty advisor. If this is not the same faculty member as the course instructor, the faculty advisor will coordinate with the course instructor when it comes to assessing the student’s research process at the end of each quarter.

LSCI 195B.title: Language Science Research II
LSCI 195B.description: Provides students with in-depth experience in different facets of research in language science. It includes theoretical, behavioral, computational, and/or applied language science topics and methodologies.
LSCI 195B.prereq_text: Permission of faculty advisor. If this is not the same faculty member as the course instructor, the faculty advisor will coordinate with the course instructor when it comes to assessing the student’s research process at the end of each quarter.

LSCI 195C.title: Language Science Research III
LSCI 195C.description: Provides students with in-depth experience in different facets of research in language science. It includes theoretical, behavioral, computational, and/or applied language science topics and methodologies.
LSCI 195C.prereq_text: Permission of faculty advisor. If this is not the same faculty member as the course instructor, the faculty advisor will coordinate with the course instructor when it comes to assessing the student’s research process at the end of each quarter.

LSCI 195W.title: Writing Skills for Language Science
LSCI 195W.description: Focuses on written technical communication skills in language science. Topics include the scientific publication process (focusing on research abstracts), how to write for pieces of different lengths, and writing for different audiences.

LSCI 199.title: Independent Study
LSCI 199.description: Independent research with Linguistics faculty. Students may enroll for only one 199 each quarter.

LSCI 201A.title: Topics in Language Science Research
LSCI 201A.description: Involves colloquia and scientific reports by faculty, students, and visitors. Students are exposed to current language science research and gain experience in active listening and scientific discourse.

LSCI 201B.title: Topics in Language Science Research
LSCI 201B.description: Involves colloquia and scientific reports by faculty, students, and visitors. Students are exposed to current language science research and gain experience in active listening and scientific discourse.

LSCI 201C.title: Topics in Language Science Research
LSCI 201C.description: Involves colloquia and scientific reports by faculty, students, and visitors. Students are exposed to current language science research and gain experience in active listening and scientific discourse.

LSCI 202A.title: Skills for Language Science I
LSCI 202A.description: Focuses on computational skills for language science research. Topics include computational literacy, programming languages, and database interfaces that are useful for language science research, allowing for general scripting and file manipulation, and enabling statistical analysis and data visualization.

LSCI 202B.title: Skills for Language Science II
LSCI 202B.description: Introduction to the scientific publication process and practice of scientific writing skills.
LSCI 202B.prereq_text: LSCI 202A with a minimum grade of B-.

LSCI 202C.title: Skills for Language Science III
LSCI 202C.description: Introduction to scientific presentation for audiences of different backgrounds and practice of scientific presentations skills.
LSCI 202C.prereq_text: LSCI 202B with a minimum grade of B-.

LSCI 202D.title: Advanced Skills for Language Science
LSCI 202D.description: The practice of advanced professional writing skills, including the writing of grants. Students bring their own academic material to the workshop.
LSCI 202D.prereq_text: LSCI 202C with a minimum grade of B.

LSCI 202E.title: Advanced Skills for Language Science II
LSCI 202E.description: The practice of advanced professional writing skills, including the writing of research statements and related documents. Students bring their own academic material to the workshop.
LSCI 202E.prereq_text: LSCI 202D with a minimum grade of B.

LSCI 202F.title: Advanced Skills for Language Science III
LSCI 202F.description: The practice of advanced professional writing skills, including the writing of journal articles. Students bring their own academic material to the workshop.
LSCI 202F.prereq_text: LSCI 202E with a minimum grade of B.

LSCI 206C.title: Computational Models of Language Learning
LSCI 206C.description: Focuses on computational models of native language learning, exploring how probabilistic learning and inference fare on difficult case studies within language acquisition. In all cases, grounds the learning models in available empirical data and considers their psychological plausibility.
LSCI 206C.prereq_text: LSCI 251 with a minimum grade of B-.

LSCI 209.title: Special Topics in Computational Linguistics
LSCI 209.description: Focuses on ongoing research in linguistics. Variable units based on course content, as determined by Department. May be repeated for credit as topic varies.

LSCI 217.title: Introduction to Acoustic Phonetics
LSCI 217.description: Introduction to the study of the acoustic properties of speech and their relationship to speech articulation and speech perception. Topics covered include making and interpreting quantitative acoustic measurements of speech, basic experimental design, and basic data visualization and statistical analysis.

LSCI 219.title: Special Topics in Phonetics and Phonology

LSCI 248M.title: Modal Logic
LSCI 248M.description: Introduction to modal logic methods and their application.

LSCI 250.title: Psycholinguistics
LSCI 250.description: Examines how language is used in real time, and how its use reveals how it is represented in the mind and the brain.

LSCI 250B.title: Bilingualism
LSCI 250B.description: Examines how bilingualism interfaces with language representation, language use, and language development.

LSCI 250H.title: Heritage Language Acquistion
LSCI 250H.description: Examines how heritage languages are represented in speakers' minds, processed in real time, and acquired.

LSCI 251.title: Language Acquisition
LSCI 251.description: Focuses on native language learning, exploring the way in which infants and very young children unconsciously uncover the rich systematic knowledge of their native language. Examines both experimental and computational studies that quantitatively investigate the "how" of language acquisition.

LSCI 251A.title: Atypical Acquisition
LSCI 251A.description: Focuses on different types of atypical acquisition, including acquisition in special populations and acquisition under atypical circumstances. Research techniques discussed include theoretical, experimental, and computational methods.

LSCI 251C.title: Computational Cognitive Models of Language Acquistion
LSCI 251C.description: Focuses on synthesizing research literature related to computational cognitive models of language acquisition. Students develop their abilities to discuss key concepts and background assumptions, clearly present major points and findings, and concisely summarize literature from a particular perspective.

LSCI 253M.title: Experimental Methods for Language Research
LSCI 253M.description: Focuses on experimental methods useful for language research. Students become familiar with software and programming languages used for implementing and analyzing behavioral experiments.

LSCI 259.title: Special Topics in Psycholinguistics
LSCI 259.description: Topics in Psycholinguistics. May be repeated for credit as topic varies.

LSCI 265L.title: Language Change, Acquisition, and Complexity
LSCI 265L.description: Focuses on models of language change, acquisition, and complexity, looking at the connections between them to explain empirical data relating to the form of existing languages and how languages change over time. Emphasis is placed on computational and mathematical models.

LSCI 281L.title: Language Learning with Digital Media
LSCI 281L.description: Provides students with a graduate-level introduction to key issues of digital media in second-language teaching and learning.

LSCI 281S.title: Second Language Acquisition and Teaching
LSCI 281S.description: Explores the prevailing paradigms that seek to account for how adults learn second languages (L2s) in instructed settings.

LSCI 299.title: Independent Study
LSCI 299.description: Independent study. Research with language science faculty.

M&MG 200A.title: Research in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 200A.description: Individual research supervised by a particular professor.

M&MG 200B.title: Research in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 200B.description: Individual research supervised by a particular professor.
M&MG 200B.prereq_text: M&MG 200A with a minimum grade of B-.

M&MG 200C.title: Research in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 200C.description: Individual research supervised by a particular professor.
M&MG 200C.prereq_text: M&MG 200B with a minimum grade of B-.

M&MG 200R.title: Research in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics for First-Year Students
M&MG 200R.description: Independent research within the laboratories of graduate training faculty in the Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics for first-year Ph.D. students.

M&MG 201A.title: Research topics in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 201A.description: Seminars presented by graduate students and faculty of the Department which explore research topics in specialized areas of microbiology and molecular genetics. Opportunity for students to gain experience in the organization, critical evaluation, and oral presentation of current research developments.

M&MG 201B.title: Research topics in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 201B.description: Seminars presented by graduate students and faculty of the Department which explore research topics in specialized areas of microbiology and molecular genetics. Oppurtunity for students to gain experience in the organization, critical evaluation, and oral presentation of current research developments.
M&MG 201B.prereq_text: M&MG 201A with a minimum grade of B-.

M&MG 201C.title: Research topics in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 201C.description: Seminars presented by graduate students and faculty of the Department which explore research topics in specialized areas of microbiology and molecular genetics. Oppurtunity for students to gain experience in the organization, critical evaluation, and oral presentation of current research developments.
M&MG 201C.prereq_text: M&MG 201B with a minimum grade of B-.

M&MG 203A.title: Advanced Studies in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 203A.description: Organized within each laboratory group, one to four hours. Advanced study in areas related to faculty research interests. Involves small group study based on readings, discussions, and guest speakers. May be conducted as journal clubs.

M&MG 203B.title: Advanced Studies in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 203B.description: Organized within each laboratory group, one to four hours. Advanced study in areas related to faculty research interests. Involves small group study based on readings, discussions, and guest speakers. May be conducted as journal clubs.

M&MG 203C.title: Advanced Studies in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 203C.description: Organized within each laboratory group, one to four hours. Advanced study in areas related to faculty research interests. Involves small group study based on readings, discussions, and guest speakers. May be conducted as journal clubs.
M&MG 203C.prereq_text: M&MG 203B with a minimum grade of B-.

M&MG 206.title: Regulation of Gene Expression
M&MG 206.description: Aspects of gene expression including the organization of the eukaryotic nucleus in terms of protein-nucleic acid interaction (i.e., chromatin and chromosome structure); the enzymology and regulation of RNA transcription and pre-mRNA processing in eukaryotes; mechanisms of RNAi and translation.

M&MG 210A.title: Medical Microbiology
M&MG 210A.description: Biology of microbial pathogens (viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites) as foundation for subsequent study of infectious diseases. Topics: molecular basis of microbial pathogenesis; clinical presentation and epidemiology; diagnostic testing; antimicrobial therapy; prevention strategies. Format: lectures, laboratory, clinical cases, liveclasstech interactive questions.

M&MG 215B.title: Integrative Immunology II
M&MG 215B.description: Lectures and student presentations of primary literature. Focuses on advanced topics and cutting edge technologies in modern immunology. Combination of didactic lectures and student-led journal article discussion.
M&MG 215B.prereq_text: PHYSIO 215 with a minimum grade of B+.

M&MG 221.title: Immunopathogenic Mechanisms of Disease
M&MG 221.description: Examination of the mechanisms underlying disease states mediated by immune dysregulation including mechanisms of immune evasion by cancer, diseases mediated by cytokine dysregulation, role of the microbiome of the GI tract and of other disease sites, and adoptive T-cell (CAR-T-cells).
M&MG 221.restriction: Campus Honors Collegium students and juniors and seniors may audit.

M&MG 222.title: Molecular Pathogenesis of Microbial Infections
M&MG 222.description: Features lectures by faculty on the molecular aspects of microbial pathogenesis, highlighting both microbe and cellular functions. In addition to lectures, students review papers and discuss them. There will be two written exams, one on viruses and one on microbes.

M&MG 225.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Human Disease
M&MG 225.description: Provides an overview of the molecular mechanisms of human diseases, including neurologic, hematologic, neoplastic, and infectious diseases. Students gain an understanding of these mechanisms, as well as models of human diseases.

M&MG 230.title: Topics in Stem Cells
M&MG 230.description: One-hour seminar presentation by participating faculty or guest lecturer and open to the science community, followed by one-hour discussion of the lecture topic or related topic. Students are responsible for presentations and readings.

M&MG 240.title: M.D./PH.D. Tutorial
M&MG 240.description: Explores a variety of topics that impact careers of medical scientists (M.D./Ph.D students). Topics range from scientific, such as recent advances in particular research areas, to ethical problems brought on by increased technology and intervention in the disease process.

M&MG 250.title: Responsible Conduct of Research
M&MG 250.description: Each session includes a formal presentation by faculty/invited speaker followed by a discussion of case studies related to the topic under consideration.

M&MG 270.title: Career Development
M&MG 270.description: Topics include preparation of papers, grants and fellowships, scientific presentations, and curriculum vitae, and career opportunities.

M&MG 280.title: Tutorial in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 280.description: Tutorial in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics. Presented by the department faculty; relates current laboratory research to the literature.

M&MG 292A.title: Scientific Communication
M&MG 292A.description: Small group meetings for graduate students to practice scientific writing, debate, and presentation skills.

M&MG 292B.title: Scientific Communication
M&MG 292B.description: Small group meetings for graduate students to practice scientific writing, debate, and presentation skills.

M&MG 292C.title: Scientific Communication
M&MG 292C.description: Small group meetings for graduate students to practice scientific writing, debate, and presentation skills.

M&MG 298.title: Independent Study
M&MG 298.description: Provided for MSTP students to synthesize the basic science information learned during the basic science years of medical school and learn how to apply that knowledge toward graduate research directed at understanding the basis of human disease.

M&MG 299.title: Dissertation—Microbiology and Molecular Genetics
M&MG 299.description: Course provided for Ph.D. students to prepare and complete the dissertation required for a Ph.D. degree.

MATH 1A.title: Pre-Calculus I
MATH 1A.description: Basic equations and inequalities, linear and quadratic functions, and systems of simultaneous equations.

MATH 1B.title: Pre-Calculus II
MATH 1B.description: Preparation for calculus and other mathematics courses. Exponentials, logarithms, trigonometry, polynomials, and rational functions. Satisfies no requirements other than contribution to the 180 units required for graduation.
MATH 1B.prereq_text: Recommended: A passing score on the Pre-Calculus Self-Assessment exam, or a score of 450 or higher on the Mathematics section of the SAT Reasoning Test. Not for students with a score of 3 or higher on the AP Calc AB exam. Not for students with a score of 3 or higher on the AP Calc BC exam.
MATH 1B.restriction: Economics majors, Quantitative Economics majors, Business Economics majors, Pharmaceutical Sciences majors, Public Health Sciences majors, School of Physical Sciences students, School of Information and Computer Sciences students, School of Engineering students, Division of Undergraduate Education students, and School of Business students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 2A.title: Single-Variable Calculus I
MATH 2A.description: Introduction to derivatives, calculation of derivatives of algebraic and trigonometric functions; applications including curve sketching, related rates, and optimization. Exponential and logarithm functions.

and.not: AP CALCULUS AB score of 3 or greater
AP CALCULUS BC score of 3 or greater
AP CALCULUS AB SUB score of 3 or greater

MATH 2A.prereq_text: MATH 1B with a minimum grade of C- or SAT Mathematics with a minimum score of 650 or ACT Mathematics with a minimum score of 29. Placement via the Calculus Placement exam (fee required) is also accepted.
MATH 2A.restriction: School of Physical Sciences students, School of Engineering students, School of Information and Computer Sciences students, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 2AX.title: Calculus Preparation
MATH 2AX.description: Group activities designed to review and reinforce fundamental concepts essential for success in Calculus. Linear functions, quadratic functions, polynomials, and rational functions; exponentials and logarithms; trigonometry; absolute values. Graphs of functions.

MATH 2B.title: Single-Variable Calculus II
MATH 2B.description: Definite integrals; the fundamental theorem of calculus. Applications of integration including finding areas and volumes. Techniques of integration. Infinite sequences and series.
MATH 2B.prereq_text: MATH 2A or MATH 5A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 3.
MATH 2B.restriction: Unaffiliated Undeclared majors, School of Physical Sciences students, School of Engineering students, School of Information and Computer Sciences students, and School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 2BX.title: Calculus Preparation II
MATH 2BX.description: Group activities designed to review and reinforce fundamental concepts essential for success in integral calculus. Differentiation and integration techniques, review of trigonometric functions, sequences and series, Taylor and power series. To be taken concurrently with MATH 2B.

MATH 2D.title: Multivariable Calculus I
MATH 2D.description: Differential and integral calculus of real-valued functions of several real variables, including applications. Polar coordinates.
MATH 2D.prereq_text: MATH 2B or MATH 5B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4.
MATH 2D.restriction: Unaffiliated Undeclared majors, School of Physical Sciences students, School of Engineering students, and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 2E.title: Multivariable Calculus II
MATH 2E.description: The differential and integral calculus of vector-valued functions. Implicit and inverse function theorems. Line and surface integrals, divergence and curl, theorems of Greens, Gauss, and Stokes.
MATH 2E.restriction: School of Physical Sciences students and School of Engineering students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 3A.title: Introduction to Linear Algebra
MATH 3A.description: Systems of linear equations, matrix operations, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, vector spaces, subspaces, and dimension.
MATH 3A.prereq_text: MATH 2B or MATH 5B or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 4.
MATH 3A.restriction: Unaffiliated Undeclared majors, Quantitative Economics majors, School of Physical Sciences students, School of Engineering students, and School of Information and Computer Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 3D.title: Elementary Differential Equations
MATH 3D.description: Linear differential equations, variation of parameters, constant coefficient cookbook, systems of equations, Laplace transforms, series solutions.
MATH 3D.restriction: Computer Science and Engineering majors, School of Physical Sciences students, and School of Engineering students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 5A.title: Calculus for Life Sciences I
MATH 5A.description: Differential calculus with applications to life sciences. Exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions. Limits, differentiation techniques, optimization and difference equations.

and.not: AP CALCULUS AB score of 3 or greater
AP CALCULUS BC score of 3 or greater
AP CALCULUS AB SUB score of 3 or greater

MATH 5A.prereq_text: MATH 1B with a minimum grade of C- or SAT Mathematics with a minimum score of 650 or ACT Mathematics with a minimum score of 29. Placement via the Calculus Placement exam (fee required) is also accepted.
MATH 5A.restriction: School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 5B.title: Calculus for Life Sciences II
MATH 5B.description: Integral calculus and multivariable calculus with applications to life sciences. Integration techniques, applications of the integral, phase plane methods and basic modeling, basic multivariable methods.
MATH 5B.prereq_text: MATH 5A or MATH 2A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 3.
MATH 5B.restriction: School of Biological Sciences students have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 8.title: Explorations in Functions and Modeling
MATH 8.description: Explorations of applications and connections in topics in algebra, geometry, calculus, and statistics for future secondary math educators. Emphasis on nonstandard modeling problems.
MATH 8.prereq_text: MATH 2A or MATH 5A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3.
MATH 8.restriction: Applied and Computational Mathematics majors and Mathematics majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 9.title: Introduction to Programming for Numerical Analysis
MATH 9.description: Introduction to computers and programming using Matlab and Python. Representation of numbers and precision, input/output, functions, custom data types, testing/debugging, reading exceptions, plotting data, numerical differentiation, basics of algorithms. Analysis of random processes using computer simulations.
MATH 9.prereq_text: MATH 2A or MATH 5A or AP Calculus AB with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus BC with a minimum score of 3 or AP Calculus AB Subscore with a minimum score of 3.
MATH 9.restriction: Applied and Computational Mathematics majors and Mathematics majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 10.title: Introduction to Programming for Data Science
MATH 10.description: Introduction to Python for data science. Selecting appropriate data types; functions and methods; plotting; the libraries NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn. Foundations of machine learning.
MATH 10.restriction: Mathematics majors and Applied and Computational Mathematics majors have the first consideration for enrollment.

MATH 13.title: Introduction to Abstract Mathematics
